newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa calls U.S. "bullyboy" over Syria deal.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa calls U.S. "bullyboy" over Syria deal.

text.p: South Africa's ruling party accused the United States on Monday of "bullyboy" tactics and hypocrisy for threatening the government over a proposed arms deal with Syria.
President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) was angered by a U.S. threat to cut off some $120 million in aid if South Africa sells tank-gun aiming controls to Syria.

Cheryl Carolus, the party's acting secretary general, told a news conference Washington was trying to force South Africa into a biased policy towards the Middle East by favouring Israel over the Arab states.

"We take strong exception to any country acting like a bullyboy in trying to, essentially, usurp our own foreign policy-making capacity," said Carolus, summarising the party's position after a summit of the ANC's executive at the weekend.

"The United States has itself contributed in a very biased way in the region (by supporting Israel) and that in itself creates problems...It's really a bit much and self-righteous to then try to speak to other people about that."
Her remarks echoed statements from Mandela and his likely successor, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, that South Africa would decided itself who to sell arms to.
The United States, which gives its close ally Israel $1.8 billion in annual military grants, calls Syria a sponsor of terrorism.
South Africa has said companies in at least three European countries are also bidding for the $650 million Syrian contract and a U.S. defence contractor is involved in at least one of those bids.

"That kind of hypocrisy of the United States -- to not do anything about that aspect of it -- we found quite disturbing, and out of keeping with the role which we would hope that a major power such as the United States would play," Carolus said.
Mbeki is to tell the South African cabinet at its first regular meeting of the year on Wednesday whether or not he favours the deal.

The opposition National Party of former president F.W. de Klerk urged him to veto the deal, saying it went against the government's own guidelines on not selling arms to troublespots and jeopardised relations with Washington. The previous white government had close military ties with Israel.
